input.query: comparison of the Croatian cybernetic machine translation program with contemporary machine translation research in the US and USSR

output.reason: The evidence fully supports the comparison. It states Croatian research was poorly funded and lagging only a couple of years behind the superpowers; that unlike US/USSR colleagues, Laszlo's group worked without an actual computer so results remained mainly theoretical; that US had prototype efforts from 1954 and USSR efforts from 1955 while Croatian group began 1958; that the USSR's information-theoretic (cybernetic) approach of Lyapunov, Kulagina and Dobrushin was the main role model for Croatian efforts from 1957; and that the Croatian approach differed from the usual logical approaches of the period, advocating cybernetic methods. The abstract also notes it explores their work in connection with MT beginnings in the USA and USSR motivated by Cold War intelligence needs.

claims.text: The paper explores Croatian machine translation work in connection with the beginnings of machine translation in the USA and USSR, motivated by the Cold War and intelligence needs of the period.

The Croatian group's approach to machine translation was different from the usual logical approaches of the period, and Laszlo advocated cybernetic methods that would be adopted as a canon by the mainstream AI community only decades later.

In the USSR there were four major approaches to machine translation in the late 1950s, including experimental work at the Institute for Precise Mechanics and Computational Technology (German-Russian prototype by 1959) and a mainly logical approach at the Steklov Mathematical Institute led by A. A. Reformatsky.
The Lyapunov, Kulagina and Dobrushin approach was mainly information-theoretic (considered cybernetic at that time) and served as the main role model for the Croatian efforts from 1957 onwards.

Laszlo and Petrović commented on the state of the art, noting USA prototype efforts from 1954, a 1955 collection of research papers, USSR efforts starting from 1955, and a UK prototype from 1956, though they did not detail or cite these articles.
The authors conclude that the poorly funded Croatian research was lagging only a couple of years behind the research of the superpowers, which invested heavily in this effort.
Unlike their colleagues in the USA and the USSR, Laszlo's group had to manage without an actual computer, and their results remained mainly theoretical.
Laszlo and Petrović note that research in computational linguistics was mainly a top-priority military effort in other countries.

Although machine translation in 1950s Croatia did not significantly influence the development of the field, it shows that Croatian linguists had contemporary views and necessary competencies, but development stopped due to previously discussed circumstances.
